content: To complement existing laws and regulations, procurement documents must include specific elements related to public health pesticide procurement as outlined in this document. National regulations should mandate that suppliers sign a declaration affirming they are not involved in bribery practices. Any violation of this declaration by the supplier should result in penalties. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) adopted the Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions in 1997, requiring signatory countries to criminalize bribery of foreign public officials under their laws. Effective procurement planning requires relevant information and realistic timelines. The selection of pesticide type, quantity, and quality should follow the criteria and procedures outlined in sections 3 and 4 of this document. Planning should begin at least six months, preferably 12 months, before the anticipated delivery date, depending on the country’s administrative and bureaucratic systems. Additional time may be necessary if multiple countries are on similar implementation cycles, allowing suppliers sufficient time to deliver products. Delivery locations and schedules should be planned in advance, considering local storage and transport availability, especially for bulky products like mosquito nets that require significant storage space. Various procurement methods can be employed, depending on the total value, product availability, and funding source. National and international procurement agencies have specific requirements for goods and services procurement. Depending on the product’s value and availability, the tendering process may be open, restricted, or limited. National regulations or funding agencies often set threshold values, above which open tendering is mandatory, and below which restricted or limited procurement is acceptable. The three procurement methods are: 1. Open tender: Open to all suppliers, also referred to as competitive or public tender. 2. Restricted or limited tender: Only shortlisted suppliers with a proven record of quality and delivery are invited. 3. Direct procurement: Products are purchased directly from a single supplier at the quoted price. To reduce dependency on a single supplier, some procurement entities may split the tender, awarding portions of the required quantities to two or more suppliers. While this minimizes the risk of supplier default, it may increase prices. Countries may consider appointing a qualified external agency to assist in fair and sound procurement of public health pesticide products. International organizations such as UNICEF, the World Bank, and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria have their own procurement requirements and procedures. Tender documents should be prepared based on the country’s legal provisions for goods and services procurement, including those specific to pesticides. These documents typically consist of three sections: 1. Section 1: Information on the procurement procedure, including instructions to tenderers, conditions of tenders, and technical specifications of the products being procured. 2. Section 2: Schedule of requirements, such as time, quantity, and place of delivery. 3. Section 3: Description of the procurement contract. Instructions to tenderers should outline the procurement process and required actions to comply with the requirements. These instructions must adhere to legal procurement requirements and include the scope of the tender, submission procedures, opening and evaluation processes, and contract award criteria. Open tenders are often advertised in newspapers, international journals, or online to promote competition and secure the best possible price for pesticides. Personnel responsible for drafting these specifications must have appropriate expertise and experience. Incomplete or inappropriate specifications in tenders and procurement documents can lead to issues with pesticide use. Specifications should include the formulation type, relevant chemical and physical properties, acceptable impurity levels, storage stability requirements, and compliance with WHO specifications, if applicable. For long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), specifications should include details such as fiber type, impregnation technology, color, size, shape, active ingredient retention, seam stitching, netting mesh size, dimensional stability, and storage stability at elevated temperatures. Packaging requirements should specify the type, material thickness, size, and durability suitable for local use and climatic conditions. Packaging must comply with United Nations recommendations for transporting hazardous goods. LLINs should be individually packed in sealed plastic bags and baled, with secondary outer packaging for protection during transit. Labels should include essential information such as product name, active ingredients, usage instructions, storage and disposal guidelines, supplier identification, and release date. Suppliers must provide evidence of their legal and financial standing, technical expertise, and ability to produce products that meet national or WHO specifications. Local suppliers sourcing pesticides from abroad must demonstrate that the products come from capable and reliable manufacturers. Delivery schedules and locations must be specified in the tender documents. The procurement entity has the right to examine and sample the supplied products. If the products are of unacceptable quality or improperly packaged or labeled, the supplier must replace them at their own cost or refund the procurement entity. Suppliers may also be required to collect empty pesticide containers for proper disposal, provide protective gear and training, and offer technical support. WHO specifications provide an international reference for evaluating pesticide quality. Suppliers must provide a certificate of analysis for each product batch at delivery. Independent quality control involves selecting a certified or accredited laboratory, random sampling, and analysis to verify compliance with specifications. The laboratory conducting the analysis must be independent of the supplier and adhere to ISO 17025 accreditation standards or equivalent.
